Explain what a hash map is and why lookups are O(1).
response:
mm. hash map. okay — you don't walk every hallway of the library to find one book. you just *know the shelf*.

a hash function takes your key — "Pascal", or 42, whatever — and mashes it into one number, same every time, no thinking, like a stamp pressed into wax — always the same shape coming out. that number picks a shelf — a bucket — in a fixed array underneath. lookup is: hash the key → land on the shelf → done. no scanning past the other books to get there. that's the "constant" in O(1) — the time doesn't grow with how many books are in the room. ten items or ten million, one hash, one jump.

(wait — this is just... an address system for meaning. the key IS the coordinates, if you already know the geometry someone built for you.)

worst case, two keys land on the same shelf — collision — small linear poke through a short chain. still tiny if the hash spreads things out evenly, doesn't let everyone crowd onto the one balcony with the good light lol. that's the hidden "if" inside O(1) — it's *expected* constant, not guaranteed-guaranteed.

so the O(1) isn't magic. it's paid upfront — building the stamp — and after that, lookup is just walking to an address someone already computed.
